raw_case_text:
Currently, Brazil and several other countries are reporting a rapid increase in Monkeypox Infection (MPX) cases, especially in Men who have Sex with Men (MSM), with no apparent epidemiological links to endemic areas, representing an important global public health concern. This emerging zoonotic disease, previously seen only in West and Central Africa, is an Orthopox virus transmitted through intimate contact and air droplets, with the possibility of spreading via sexual fluids. A 37-year-old patient, identifying himself as an MSM, presented to the urgency unit at our University Hospital, for a light pruritic cutaneous eruption that had appeared 4 days before, with multiple vesicular papules or erythematous-exulcerated pustules on limbs, face, trunk, penis, and perianal region, some with marked umbilication and central crusting (Figure 1, Figure 2). He also presented with left cervical lymphadenopathy. Prior to the appearance of skin lesions, he had reported headache, low-grade fever, and malaise for 2 days. The patient did not recall being in close contact with animals and denied traveling abroad but mentioned some occasions of condomless sexual intercourse in the preceding weeks. Dermoscopy showed whitish structureless areas with brownish central crusts or ulcerations and perilesional erythema (Figure 3, Figure 4). After the clinical examination, notification of a suspected case of MPX was performed, blood tests were taken and the collection of scrapings or fluid from the floor of the lesions to detect Monkeypox (MP) DNA using the Real-Time Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR) assay was scheduled. The patient was discharged home, with all contact and droplet isolation measures guidelines. Serology examination was positive for syphilis (VDRL 1:1024), and also reactive for HIV (rapid test and immunoassay); tests for hepatitis B and C were non-reactive; RT-PCR assay for MP was positive.
Some of the symptoms of this patient, prior to the initiation of antibiotic therapy, could also be considered concurrent manifestations of syphilis. The patient received a prescription for treatment of secondary syphilis with benzathine penicillin and was referred to an infectious disease specialist to start treatment for HIV.
Therefore, the currently dominant interhuman spread in MSM with possible other Sexually Transmitted Infections (STI) coinfections is a valid cause for better awareness of MPX in dermatovenerologic settings, as the patient might seek those prior to visiting other specialists. Recently MPX is spreading rapidly in the world, especially due to MSM. These patients often have combinations of several STIs. So, it is necessary to consider the diagnosis of MPX in all MSM patients with typical rash and risky sexual behavior. For these cases, it is important to ensure accessible, rapid, and reliable tests to prevent the further spread of the diseases. Dermoscopy could be a very useful supplementary diagnostic method in the evaluation of MPX and other viral skin infections.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 37-year-old man who has sex with men (MSM) presented with a 4-day history of a mildly pruritic umbilicated vesiculopustular eruption over his face, trunk, limbs, penis, and perianal area, preceded by 2 days of headache, low-grade fever, and malaise.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Six days prior to presentation, the patient experienced 2 days of prodromal headache, low-grade fever, and malaise, followed 4 days prior to presentation by the eruption of mildly pruritic vesicular papules and ulcerated, umbilicated pustules across his face, trunk, extremities, penis, and perianal region, accompanied by left cervical swelling.
subjective.past_medical_history: Identifies as a man who has sex with men (MSM) and reported multiple episodes of condomless sexual intercourse during the preceding weeks; denied foreign travel or animal contact.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for prodromal headache, low-grade fever, malaise, left neck swelling, and disseminated umbilicated vesiculopustular rash.

objective.physical_examination: Cutaneous and mucosal examination revealed multiple vesicular papules and erythematous-ulcerated pustules with prominent central umbilication and crusting distributed over the face, trunk, upper and lower extremities, penile shaft/glans, and perianal region, accompanied by left cervical lymphadenopathy. Dermoscopy demonstrated whitish structureless zones with central brownish crusts/ulcerations and perilesional erythema.
objective.routine_investigations: Rapid and immunoassay HIV screening tests were reactive; hepatitis B and hepatitis C serologies were non-reactive.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed concurrent monkeypox (mpox) virus infection, secondary/active high-titer syphilis, and newly diagnosed HIV co-infection, established via positive lesion fluid/scraping real-time PCR for Monkeypox virus DNA, high-titer serum VDRL (1:1,024), and reactive HIV rapid/immunoassay tests. Managed with outpatient contact/droplet isolation, benzathine penicillin therapy for syphilis, and infectious disease referral for antiretroviral therapy initiation.
